summary: For ages 7–9, learners identify the three main cloud types — cumulus (fluffy, fair-weather, low), stratus (flat grey overcast layers that can bring drizzle) and cirrus (thin high icy wisps) — and learn that clouds form when water vapour cools and condenses into tiny liquid droplets (or, very high up where it is freezing, tiny ice crystals). Identification works best from real sky photos paired with altitude, and each type links to a simple, checkable weather prediction. The commonest misconception to confront directly is that a visible cloud is water vapour or gas; in fact vapour is invisible and the visible cloud is tiny liquid droplets or ice crystals.
misconceptions: Clouds are made of water vapour or gas — visible clouds are tiny LIQUID (or ice) droplets; vapour is invisible
Steam is water vapour — it is condensed liquid droplets too
In a cloud-in-a-jar demo, the smoke IS the cloud — the smoke provides particles for droplets to condense on
Clouds are solid/fluffy things you could stand on, rather than suspended droplets
All clouds mean rain — many (cumulus, cirrus) are fair-weather or high-and-dry

activities.title: Altitude-layered sky field guide
steps: Study one rich sky scene showing cirrus streaking high, cumulus billowing low, and a flat grey stratus sheet, and notice how the three types sit at different heights.

For each cloud, record its name, what it looks like, roughly how high it sits, and the weather it signals (cirrus: thin icy wisps, very high, a change may be coming; cumulus: fluffy, low, usually fair weather; stratus: flat grey layer, overcast, often bringing drizzle).
Reveal a 'What weather?' forecast for each cloud, then whenever you spot that cloud type in the real sky over the coming days, check whether the predicted weather follows.
Zoom into one cloud to see a model of invisible water vapour cooling and condensing onto tiny particles to form droplets, and state in your own words what the cloud is actually made of.
activities.insight: Clouds are not random blobs but a named, layered system you can read by look and height; and a visible cloud is made of tiny liquid droplets or ice crystals, not invisible vapour.

activities.title: Sort real sky photographs
steps: Collect or view a set of real sky photographs and sort each one into cumulus, stratus or cirrus.
For each photo, name one feature that decided your choice (fluffy and piled, flat grey layer, or thin high wisps).
Group the sorted photos by the weather each type tends to bring and explain the pattern.
activities.insight: Real skies are messier than diagrams; applying the look-and-height features to genuine photos builds reliable recognition and connects type to likely weather.

activities.title: Cool-the-air cloud formation
steps: Use a control that cools a pocket of air and watch invisible water vapour condense into a visible cloud of droplets as the temperature drops.
Describe the sequence: warm air holds invisible vapour, cooling makes the vapour condense onto tiny particles, and the gathered droplets become the cloud you can see.
Relate this to everyday examples such as breath fogging on a cold day or steam cooling above a kettle — both are condensed droplets, not vapour.
activities.insight: A cloud forms when cooling turns invisible water vapour into tiny liquid droplets that together become visible; the visible part is always liquid or ice, never the gas itself.

activities.title: Build a class cloud log
steps: Observe and photograph (or sketch) the sky at a set time across a week and name the cloud type each day.
Beside each entry, note the weather that followed and compare it with what that cloud type predicts.
At the end of the week, review which predictions held and discuss why a cloud type signals the weather it does.
activities.insight: Cloud identification is an observational skill: watching real skies over time links cloud type to weather and shows prediction can be tested.

activities.title: Check recognition and prediction
steps: Match each cloud image to its name (cumulus, stratus, cirrus).
Answer: which cloud is made mostly of ice crystals? (cirrus), and which sky — tall dark piled-up clouds or thin high wisps — is more likely to bring rain soon?
Explain in a sentence what a cloud is actually made of.
activities.insight: Confirms the learner can name types from images, pick out the ice-cloud discriminator, and read cloud shape as a rain signal while stating the condensation model.

activities.title: Ask a weather watcher
steps: Pose questions to a knowledgeable adult or imagined meteorologist, such as 'What does that cloud mean?' or 'Why do those two clouds bring different weather?'
Explain back, in your own words, the reasoning behind one answer.
activities.insight: Talking through what a cloud signals deepens understanding of the type-to-weather link and invites reasoning, though the recognition itself still rests on seeing the clouds.

checkQuestion: One day you see thick, tall clouds with dark bottoms piling up like cauliflowers. Another day, thin wispy streaks sit high in the sky. What is a cloud actually made of, and which sky is more likely to bring rain soon?
checkAnswer: A cloud is made of tiny water droplets (and sometimes ice crystals) formed when water vapour cools and condenses. The tall, dark, piled-up cloud is far more likely to bring rain soon than the thin, high, wispy streaks.
